The last term is nonnegative, is less than 1/PN≤2−N1/P_N\le2^{-N}, and tends to zero. This is the greedy mixed-radix expansion of the fractional part of X0=S/2X_0=S/2, with digits in {0,…,29}\{0,\ldots,29\}. For the actual series its first eight digits are (δ0,…,δ7)=(1,4,8,3,10,1,8,5).(\delta_0,\ldots,\delta_7)=(1,4,8,3,10,1,8,5). To certify them, use the twelve-block enclosure from Section 11, either propagated by the recurrence or evaluated directly as Pa∑j=a11mjPj+1<Xa≤Pa∑j=a11mjPj+1+PaP12Q(n12)(0≤a<12).P_a\sum_{j=a}^{11}\frac{m_j}{P_{j+1}}<X_a \le P_a\sum_{j=a}^{11}\frac{m_j}{P_{j+1}} +\frac{P_a}{P_{12}}Q(n_{12})\qquad(0\le a<12). Both descriptions give the same rational endpoints. At indices 00 through 88 the whole interval lies strictly between consecutive integers, which certifies the floor; a small interval width alone would not suffice if the interval crossed an integer. For example, ⌊X4⌋=2\lfloor X_4\rfloor=2 and ⌊X5⌋=5\lfloor X_5\rfloor=5, giving δ4=65+5−30⋅2=10\delta_4=65+5-30\cdot2=10, not the uncarried numerator m4=65m_4=65. This finite calculation makes no claim about the later digit complexity.

A rational number need not have eventually periodic digits when the radices vary. For example, take radix 55 at the indices 1,2,4,8,…1,2,4,8,\ldots and radix 33 elsewhere. The constant tail fraction 1/21/2 gives digit 22 at those indices and 11 elsewhere. These digits are not eventually periodic, but their mixed-radix expansion sums to 1/21/2. This example uses different radices from our four possible bases; it shows why fixed-base eventual periodicity cannot be transferred to a variable-radix expansion. Our digits also depend on the actual tail fractions, not just on the four-letter radix sequence. The construction supplies neither a fixed-base expansion with verified echoing properties nor a bound on its digit complexity.

Adamczewski–Bugeaud’s complexity theorem [30] concerns the actual digits of an integer-base expansion: for an algebraic irrational their length-nn block complexity divided by nn tends to infinity. Neither (ba)(b_a) nor the uncarried (ea)(e_a) is such a digit expansion of α\alpha.

Problem 12.5 (the repeated three-prime target). Prove irrationality of S=ℛ{2,3,5}S=\mathcal R_{\{2,3,5\}}. Equivalent forms are 𝖤(K)\mathsf E(K) and BXa∉ℤfor every B≥1 with gcd⁡(B,30)=1 and every a≥1.\begin{equation} \label{long269:eq:tail-nonintegrality} BX_a\notin\mathbb Z \quad\text{for every }B\ge1\text{ with }\gcd(B,30)=1\text{ and every }a\ge1. \end{equation}

The residue formulation uses finite integer computations, but asks for a success for every eligible denominator and beyond every prescribed start. The tail formulation requires that no positive integer multiplier coprime to 3030 make any XaX_a, a≥1a\ge1, integral. These are reformulations of the same irrationality assertion, not extra assumptions on the series, and neither follows from the rank obstruction. The next proposition proves the tail reformulation, complementing Theorem 10.2.

Proposition 12.6 (irrationality is equivalent to nonintegrality of every reduced tail). Statement [long269:eq:tail-nonintegrality], quantified over every B≥1B\ge1 coprime to 3030 and every a≥1a\ge1, is equivalent to irrationality of SS.

Proof. If BXa∈ℤBX_a\in\mathbb{Z} for some such BB and aa, then Xa∈ℚX_a\in\mathbb{Q}, and since S=∑j<asj+Xa/haS=\sum_{j<a}s_j+X_a/h_a with hah_a a positive rational and the prefix a finite sum of rationals, S∈ℚS\in\mathbb{Q}. Conversely if S∈ℚS\in\mathbb{Q}, then Theorem 9.3 produces BB coprime to 3030 with BXa∈ℤBX_a\in\mathbb{Z} for every a≥aDa\ge a_D. ◻

Integrality at one index propagates forwards, but nonintegrality at one early index does not propagate forever: a rational denominator can clear later. Proposition 9.4 describes that onset exactly. The dichotomy in Proposition 8.4 also permits integral tails, so it does not settle this question.

Function-theoretic representations

The elementary proof of irrationality of 𝒟{2,3,5}\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}} gives no transcendence conclusion. Recall that 𝒟{2,3,5}=1+∑t∈{2n,3n,5n:n≥1}12⌊log⁡2t⌋3⌊log⁡3t⌋5⌊log⁡5t⌋.\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}}=1+ \sum_{t\in\{2^n,3^n,5^n:n\ge1\}} \frac1{2^{\lfloor\log_2t\rfloor}3^{\lfloor\log_3t\rfloor} 5^{\lfloor\log_5t\rfloor}}. Each running LCM is counted once at its first jump, unlike the repeated sum. The bases in [long269:eq:dyadic-alphabet] come from these same jumps. For two primes a representation by one Hecke–Mahler value proves transcendence (Section 4). A corresponding three-prime representation has not been constructed here.

Problem 12.7 (an exact function representing the distinct-height sum). Transcendence of 𝒟{2,3,5}\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}} is not proved here. For a functional approach to it, first specify the function, its coefficient field and convergence domain, then prove an exact identity for 𝒟{2,3,5}\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}}, and only then apply a stated value theorem. A conditional theorem must display the extra nondegeneracy assumption; a no-representation theorem must specify the class it excludes.

For (p,q,r)=(2,3,5)(p,q,r)=(2,3,5), the two slopes in the rank proof are log⁡52=θ5\log_5 2=\theta_5 and log⁡53=θ5/θ3\log_5 3=\theta_5/\theta_3, not θ3\theta_3 and θ5\theta_5. Each is irrational: a rational value would equate a positive power of 55 with a positive power of 22 or 33. The proof chooses the row and column indices independently. It therefore needs no rational independence of 1,θ3,θ51,\theta_3,\theta_5 and no density assertion for the singly indexed orbit ({nθ3},{nθ5})(\{n\theta_3\},\{n\theta_5\}). Any functional approach that needs such a stronger hypothesis must establish it separately.

A finite-dimensional encoding must preserve equality of the functions it is meant to represent. If two encodings agree but their functions do not, the encoding cannot justify a conclusion about those functions. The Lean sources express this condition as a factorisation through a finite-dimensional space and prove that the resulting space of functions is then finite-dimensional (identity for the carry, map to functions, finite-dimensional conclusion). They also bound the carry residue and its digit in their stated intervals (residue bound, digit bound). These conditional linear-algebra statements neither construct a function representing 𝒟{2,3,5}\mathcal D_{\{2,3,5\}} nor show that a corresponding function space must be infinite-dimensional.

The cited value theorems and their hypotheses.

Pellarin’s rank-one theorem concerns quadratic irrational slopes and algebraic evaluation points in the convergence domain . The prime-logarithm slopes used here are not quadratic: each log⁡rp\log_r p is irrational by unique factorisation, and the Gelfond–Schneider theorem then makes it transcendental, since rlog⁡rp=pr^{\log_r p}=p is algebraic.1 This rules out direct substitution of those slopes into Pellarin’s quadratic-slope theorem. It does not rule out a different representation of the scalar sum, and it does not affect the two-prime argument above, which uses a theorem for general irrational slopes.

In Pellarin’s reduced-slope normalisation, the rank-one condition says that the evaluation points arise from a common point by the quadratic order’s monomial action, up to multiplication by torsion points. For a single evaluation point it is automatic: use that point itself and the identity action. For several points it is a condition to check, not a consequence of having two lattice coordinates. Under it, algebraic independence of the values is equivalent to ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear independence of the specified auxiliary formal Laurent series; the rank-one condition alone does not imply independence. This module rank is not the rank of our reciprocal kernel. No exact representation suitable for this theorem has been constructed here, but infinite kernel rank alone does not preclude one.

For one variable, Adamczewski and Faverjon’s proofs of Nishioka’s theorem and the lifting theorem are regular-point results . Regularity means that the system matrix stays defined and invertible along the evaluation orbit. Their multivariate lifting theorem additionally assumes an admissible transformation–point pair. Its growth, decay and nonvanishing conditions are specified in Definition 5.1; none follows merely from writing a double sum. Lifting transfers a relation among values to one among functions; a transcendence application must exclude the latter. A Mahler system alone cannot do this, as the constant function 11 illustrates.

Regularity of a preselected system is not, however, a universal prerequisite for Mahler’s method. The same paper’s Theorem 1.1 treats univariate Mahler functions at algebraic points in the punctured unit disc where their values are defined, without that regularity hypothesis. The hypotheses must therefore be matched to the particular theorem being invoked. No exact Mahler representation or suitable evaluation data for this sum over distinct running LCMs are constructed here. The locators for this paper refer to its 68-page author manuscript, not the older 52-page arXiv version.

Hypotheses for auxiliary integer recurrences

For ordered primes p1<⋯<psp_1<\cdots<p_s, the interval (p1a,p1a+1)(p_1^a,p_1^{a+1}) contains at most one power of each pi>p1p_i>p_1. The radix including the final p1p_1-jump consequently belongs to {p1∏i=2spiεi:εi∈{0,1}}.\left\{p_1\prod_{i=2}^s p_i^{\varepsilon_i}: \varepsilon_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}. This finite alphabet determines neither the frequency of the radices nor the error terms in the weighted block counts. Estimates for those quantities, or for specified shifted kernels, would be additional arithmetic inputs. The conditional statements about integer recurrences below keep such inputs explicit.

Some auxiliary results explain why bounded integer approximations alone are insufficient. Here are their hypotheses in explicit form.

Let j(n)∈{2,3,5}j(n)\in\{2,3,5\} label a sequence of jumps, and suppose each label occurs. A perturbation εn\varepsilon_n in an additive abelian group has sum zero on every interval [a,b)[a,b) whose endpoints have the same label exactly when εn=u(j(n+1))−u(j(n))\varepsilon_n=u(j(n+1))-u(j(n)) for three potential values u(2),u(3),u(5)u(2),u(3),u(5). One direction follows by telescoping. Conversely, the zero-sum assumption makes ∑k<nεk\sum_{k<n}\varepsilon_k the same at any two indices with the same label. Assign that common value to u(j(n))u(j(n)); every label occurs, so all three values are defined. Consecutive partial sums then give the displayed identity. In the usual terminology, the perturbation is a coboundary of the function uu on the labels: it is the difference of successive potential values. This is a telescoping condition, not a bound on the size of the perturbation. It does not by itself force the perturbation to vanish: unequal potential values give nonzero differences when the label changes. If the perturbation also vanishes on a genuine 2→32\to3 transition and on a genuine 2→52\to5 transition, all three potential values agree, so every perturbation is zero.

For an integer sequence satisfying cn+1=bncn−Dmnc_{n+1}=b_nc_n-Dm_n, compare it with an integer sequence znz_n. Define the error en=Dzn−cne_n=Dz_n-c_n and the perturbation εn=bnzn−zn+1−mn\varepsilon_n=b_nz_n-z_{n+1}-m_n. Then en+1=bnen−Dεn.e_{n+1}=b_ne_n-D\varepsilon_n. Under the preceding zero-sum and transition hypotheses, εn=0\varepsilon_n=0 and hence eN=(∏n<Nbn)e0e_N=(\prod_{n<N}b_n)e_0. If every bn≥2b_n\ge2 and the integer e0e_0 is nonzero, then |eN|≥2N|e_N|\ge2^N. This contradicts even one bound |eN|<2N|e_N|<2^N, and therefore also excludes a uniform bound for all NN. The nonzero initial error is essential: the identically zero error causes no contradiction.

A calculation at four consecutive indices gives a related obstruction. If 0<Ti<10<T_i<1, zi∈ℤz_i\in\mathbb{Z} and |zi−Ti|<1|z_i-T_i|<1, then ziz_i is 00 or 11. For bases 2,3,2,52,3,2,5, the equalities 2z0−z1−1=02z_0-z_1-1=0 and 2z2−z3−1=02z_2-z_3-1=0 force all four integers to be 11. The sum of the first two perturbations is then (2z0−z1−1)+(3z1−z2−1)=1,(2z_0-z_1-1)+(3z_1-z_2-1)=1, not zero. Thus unit accuracy, the two exact equalities and a zero sum on that block cannot all hold. Unit accuracy alone does not give either exact equality.

No integer approximation to the tails of SS is constructed here that satisfies all these conditions. Rationality supplies integer carries of at most quadratic growth, but not the additional zero-sum and transition identities. The carries obtained from SS satisfy a weighted block identity instead. Applying the auxiliary results would require that identity to imply their hypotheses, or would require a different construction of the integer approximations.

There is also a conditional criterion for a sum supported on the powers of 22. Its elementary ingredients can be stated without introducing another formal vocabulary. From y′=by−1y'=by-1 with b>0b>0 and 0<y′<10<y'<1 one gets 1/b<y<2/b1/b<y<2/b. For integers a>0a>0 and p≥3p\ge3, if u>1/au>1/a and v<2/(pa)v<2/(pa), then u−v>1/(3a)u-v>1/(3a). Finally, a real number xx is irrational if, for every positive integer dd, there are integers n,kn,k with 0<|nx−k|<1/d0<|nx-k|<1/d.

To use these observations for a series, the conditional result requires exact identities yM=HMx−zMy_M=H_Mx-z_M, with HM,zM∈ℤH_M,z_M\in\mathbb{Z}, and, for every positive dd, two indices with different HMH_M, different yMy_M, and |yM−yM′|<1/d|y_M-y_{M'}|<1/d. Their difference gives the required nonzero linear form. Equal tail values would give zero and would not suffice; a merely bounded gap would not suffice either. Indeed, for a rational xx of denominator dd, every nonzero difference of this form has size at least 1/d1/d. No concrete series in this record is shown to satisfy all these clearing and arbitrarily small nonzero-gap conditions.

The unresolved repeated-sum question

Theorem 1.1 settles the sum over distinct running LCMs for {2,3,5}\{2,3,5\}. The ordinary arguments in Remarks 5.1 and 5.10 treat all finite prime supports and the prime-power subseries, respectively, pending formalisation. Remark 5.8 records the finite-state calculations; the collision in the admissible automaton language for {2,3,5,7}\{2,3,5,7\} limits that interval criterion only. For ℛ{2,3,5}\mathcal R_{\{2,3,5\}} we have the exact coefficients and recurrence, quadratic tail bounds and denominator-clearing formula. The remaining question is whether all eventual integral reduced tails can be excluded. Equivalently, the required residue segments must exist for every admissible BB beyond every prescribed starting index. The fixed-start formula explains the necessity of these quantifiers, and the strip identity shows why a no-crossing argument alone does not prove the required cancellation.

The rank and uniform-norm results concern the kernel, not the arithmetic of its sum. Finite tests, countability, radix recoding and denominator support do not close the remaining argument. The settled two-prime case uses Fan’s earlier reduction to the cited Hecke–Mahler value theorem.

Proof sources and declarations

Proof sources.

The margin marks retain the supplied formal-source links. A Lean mark identifies the declaration or declarations associated with a statement; a Comparator mark opens its recorded comparison. These are records of earlier checks, not fresh runs for this revision. The evidence record gives the versions and individual associations. A missing mark makes no claim of a Lean proof of the whole statement. The checks concern the propositions linked there, without establishing novelty or resolving the repeated-sum problem.

The general distinct-value assertion and its four word-and-torus arguments are stated as remarks with complete ordinary proofs in Section 5.1; they have no Lean proofs. The source record reports that the general and prime-power subseries arguments were found on 26 September 2026 and checked by a second AI agent, whose corrections were incorporated. It records no human review; the present revision does not constitute a new independent review. No separate literature search for the prime-power subseries theorem at |P|≥3|P|\ge3 is recorded, and no priority claim is made for it. The subseries identities also have ordinary proofs. The program two_tail.py checks their finite instances in exact arithmetic.

For {2,3,5}\{2,3,5\} the separate theorem for the sum over distinct values has a Lean proof; its source record says that Comparator had not been run on it. The general affine-block calculation, decoding criterion and finite-set application are also remarks with ordinary proofs; the last additionally uses exact computation. Their formal coverage is restricted to the {2,3,5}\{2,3,5\} case with one block and the interval of Section 2. The linear-flow and Smith-factor results likewise have the ordinary proofs printed here; no additional formal coverage is inferred for them.

The two-prime deduction is credited to Fan [17]. Its formal proof assumes the cited Hecke–Mahler value theorem, as specified in Section 14; its algebraic identities are unconditional. The weighted-triangle and shift identities, denominator formula, scaled dichotomy, uniqueness argument, residue limit, strip decomposition and recoding also have written proofs here. Their individual formal associations are retained, without a blanket assertion that every result in the record is formalised. Kernel acceptance uses the standard axioms allowed by the linked checks and is not an independent review of the paper-to-statement correspondence.

The twelve-block enclosure, denominator bound and eight mixed-radix digits have finite exact proofs. The two large exclusions have saved witnesses and exact checkers, and the larger scan has a saved run. None of these finite computations proves the residue inequalities beyond every starting index. No Comparator replay is claimed for the general or subseries arguments.

Artefact and data availability.

The links in the source inventory and to the integer-arithmetic checker open a fixed revision of the repository. The witnesses and exact checkers for the two large numerical exclusions and the saved larger scan are in the large-computation directory. The programs for sums over distinct values recompute the constants of Theorem 1.1 and the certificates of Remark 5.8 in exact rational arithmetic, with two independent computations of the tail intervals, and store their outputs; a fast test checks them against the stored outputs. The same directory checks the finite illustrations of Section 5.1 and the block identity for {2,3,5,7}\{2,3,5,7\}.

Further examples, conditional lemmas and source references

We collect the historical statements and then separate the lemmas on integer recurrences from their three-prime application. Their explicit divisibility and segment hypotheses specify what another recurrence must supply. Finite examples and the declaration inventory complete the record.

The historical and catalogue record

For a singleton P={p}P=\{p\}, we have an=pn−1a_n=p^{n-1} and [a1,…,an]=pn−1[a_1,\ldots,a_n]=p^{n-1}, so both sums equal p/(p−1)p/(p-1). Erdős’s 1988 account calls the infinite-prime case a simple exercise and presents irrationality for a finite number of primes greater than one as a probable extension [2]. Bloom’s catalogue records an open problem at the access date of 28 July 2026 [4]. These are dated source statements, not a fresh determination of the catalogue’s present status.

In the letter written on 1 January 1973 and published in 1974, Erdős calls the irrationality of ℛP\mathcal R_P a conjecture that he cannot prove, and says that he can show the sum over the distinct values of [a1,…,ak][a_1,\ldots,a_k] to be irrational [3]. That sum is 𝒟P\mathcal D_P. The letter introduces its primes as p1,…,psp_1,\ldots,p_s, later writing prp_r, without restricting their number, so the singleton calculation forces the qualification |P|≥2|P|\ge2. It prints no argument. The catalogue has cited the letter for Problem #269 since 28 December 2025, after the letter was quoted in the site’s discussion of missing problems [5], and its page records Erdős’s statement about the distinct values. The catalogue page says that Erdős proved the statement; the letter asserts it and prints no argument. Remark 5.1 proves it for every finite PP with |P|≥2|P|\ge2. For |P|=2|P|=2 it was already a consequence of the Hecke–Mahler transcendence theorem of Loxton and van der Poorten [16] and Bugeaud and Laurent , through the affine identity of Section 4, by the route Fan used for ℛ{p,q}\mathcal R_{\{p,q\}}. We do not know what argument Erdős had in mind.

We have not found a proof of the assertion in print. Erdős and Graham state only the question for ℛP\mathcal R_P: the sum is irrational for infinite PP, and they ask what happens for finite PP with more than one element [1]; the sum over distinct running LCMs does not appear there. Erdős’s survey of 1975 on the irrationality of series [8] does not mention the running least common multiple of the PP-smooth integers, his survey of 1980 on combinatorial number theory does not discuss irrationality, and his survey of 1988 states only the question for ℛP\mathcal R_P [2]. Every Hecke–Mahler transcendence theorem we found, including those of Loxton and van der Poorten, Bugeaud and Laurent, and Luca–Ouaknine–Worrell [26], has a single slope, and so reaches 𝒟P\mathcal D_P only for |P|=2|P|=2. The rationality criterion of Diananda and Oppenheim , which condenses a Cantor series into blocks of consecutive terms, has the form of the dyadic argument of Section 2; it restates rationality and does not decide 𝒟P\mathcal D_P. The discussion thread of Problem #269 contains no argument for 𝒟P\mathcal D_P with |P|≥3|P|\ge3, and the Formal Conjectures statement [9] concerns ℛP\mathcal R_P only. The Cantor-series criteria of Erdős–Straus [18] and Hančl–Tijdeman  do not apply to 𝒟P\mathcal D_P, as explained in Section 2. The search did not reach the sections on irrational series in Guy’s Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, or MathSciNet reviews. The unresolved target of this record is the repeated series ℛP\mathcal R_P; a transcendence statement for 𝒟P\mathcal D_P with |P|≥3|P|\ge3 is a separate question (Problem 12.7).

On 26 June 2026 Steve Fan posted the two-prime factorisation, the Hecke–Mahler reduction and the transcendence conclusion in the discussion thread of the problem’s page [17]; the comment itself notes that the argument does not seem to generalise immediately to |P|≥3|P|\ge3, and a reply there observes that it applies to arbitrary coprime pairs. The first public version of this note is dated 22 July 2026, after Fan’s post. We retain the calculation as exposition and make no priority claim for it.

The statement of the problem has been formalised as a conjecture with an unfilled proof in the Formal Conjectures collection . In the cited source, the rational, irrational and infinite-prime assertions end in sorry. Its Nat-indexed series includes the empty-prefix least-common-multiple term, so its value differs from the conventional one by a rational constant; transporting a theorem across that boundary needs an explicit series-identification lemma, which is not supplied here.

Integer recurrences in their general form

Consider an arbitrary integer recurrence with positive integer radices. Divisibility and the existence of segments satisfying the residue inequality must now be supplied as hypotheses. For the actual three-prime radices, the criterion below shows that each integer solution is eventually divisible by the smooth part of a denominator. It still leaves the residue-inequality hypothesis to be proved. The comparison with Cantor-series criteria is in Section 9.

Its valuations at 2,3,52,3,5 all tend to infinity, so every fixed DsmD_{\mathrm{sm}} eventually divides cnc_n, for any integral initial value cAc_A. Under rationality S=N/DS=N/D in lowest terms, one may start at A=1A=1: c1=DX1=N−Dc_1=DX_1=N-D is integral and coprime to DsmD_{\mathrm{sm}}. Since P1=2P_1=2, the criterion becomes Dsm∣Pn/2=hnD_{\mathrm{sm}}\mid P_n/2=h_n, exactly the onset already obtained from the finite-prefix identity in Proposition 9.4. This is an alternative proof of the divisibility step, not an additional arithmetic hypothesis left to verify for SS. The finite-prefix proof in Theorem 9.3 remains valid.

Proposition 13.2 (segments satisfying the residue inequality exclude a positive bounded integer solution). Let (bn)(b_n) and (mn)(m_n) be sequences of nonnegative integers, let G:ℕ>0×ℕ→ℕG:\mathbb{N}_{>0}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}, and assume the residue condition [long269:eq:actual-escape] for these sequences and GG, using |Wℓ,h|>0|W_{\ell,h}|>0 as the modulus. Fix B>0B>0 coprime to 3030. There is no integral sequence (dn)(d_n) satisfying simultaneously dn+1=bndn−Bmnd_{n+1}=b_nd_n-Bm_n, dn>0d_n>0 and |dn|≤G(B,n)|d_n|\le G(B,n) for every n≥0n\ge0.

Proof. Choose one segment satisfying the residue inequality (ℓ,h)(\ell,h). The iterated recurrence gives dℓ+h≡−BFℓ,hd_{\ell+h}\equiv-BF_{\ell,h} modulo |Wℓ,h||W_{\ell,h}|. The endpoint value is positive and at most G(B,ℓ+h)G(B,\ell+h), whereas the least positive residue of the right-hand side exceeds that bound, so Proposition 10.1 applies. ◻

The residue-inequality hypothesis is the substantial arithmetic assumption. It requires a residue above the bound, not just a rapidly growing product of bases. For example, the constant data bn=2b_n=2, mn=1m_n=1 have the positive solution dn=Bd_n=B. For any bound G(B,n)≥BG(B,n)\ge B, every segment has W=2hW=2^h, F=2h−1F=2^h-1 and least positive residue at most BB, so the hypothesis fails. For the actual three-prime coefficients and G=KG=K, Theorem 10.2 makes the residue-inequality hypothesis equivalent to irrationality of SS. That equivalence does not hold for an arbitrary choice of GG.

Coprimality with 3030 selects the denominators covered by the hypothesis; once a segment is fixed, the finite contradiction does not use it. The conventions cover the edge cases: a zero product of the bases is excluded, a zero residue is represented by the full modulus, and positivity prevents the endpoint value from vanishing. The version stated with a nonzero smooth factor assumes the exact factorisation cn=Dsmdnc_n=D_{\mathrm{sm}}d_n, the corresponding recurrence for (cn)(c_n) and the positive upper bound for (dn)(d_n), and gives the same contradiction.

Even retaining the actual radix sequence and quadratic growth does not force irrationality if the numerators are changed. For the same bab_a, prescribe the positive integer carries (a+3)2(a+3)^2 and set m̂a=ba(a+3)2−(a+4)2.\widehat m_a=b_a(a+3)^2-(a+4)^2. The shift by three ensures positivity even at a=0a=0: since ba≥2b_a\ge2, m̂a≥2(a+3)2−(a+4)2=a2+4a+2>0.\widehat m_a\ge2(a+3)^2-(a+4)^2=a^2+4a+2>0. Both these integer coefficients and the prescribed carries have quadratic order, because 2≤ba≤302\le b_a\le30. Nevertheless, finite telescoping gives ∑a=0N−1m̂aPa+1=9−(N+3)2PN→9.\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}\frac{\widehat m_a}{P_{a+1}} =9-\frac{(N+3)^2}{P_N}\longrightarrow9. This example keeps the exact radices, not the actual block multiplicities or their numerical upper bound QQ. It shows why the arithmetic of the specific mam_a, rather than the radix alphabet and growth orders alone, must enter a proof for SS.

Worked finite examples

At the first ten integer cutoffs, the running LCM changes by a factor 22 at 2,4,82,4,8, by 33 at 3,93,9, and by 55 at 55. The table in Section 3 also shows constant values on {5,6,7}\{5,6,7\} and {9,10}\{9,10\}, as in Proposition 3.2. In particular, L⁡(10)=8⋅9⋅5=360\operatorname{L}(10)=8\cdot9\cdot5=360 is the LCM of 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,101,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10, the supported integers at most 1010.

For Proposition 3.4 take (p,q,r)=(2,3,5)(p,q,r)=(2,3,5) and the box ℬ(1,1,1)\mathcal B(1,1,1), whose eight points carry the smooth values 1,2,3,5,6,10,15,301,2,3,5,6,10,15,30 and the running LCMs piqjrk12356101530H126606036036010800\begin{array}{c|cccccccc} p^{i}q^{j}r^{k}&1&2&3&5&6&10&15&30\\ \hline \operatorname{H}&1&2&6&60&60&360&360&10800 \end{array} Six running LCMs occur, two of them twice: the points 55 and 66 share the running LCM 6060, and 1010 and 1515 share the running LCM 360360. The identity reads 1+12+16+160+160+1360+1360+110800=1+12+16+260+2360+110800=1842110800,1+\tfrac12+\tfrac16+\tfrac1{60}+\tfrac1{60}+\tfrac1{360}+\tfrac1{360} +\tfrac1{10800} =1+\tfrac12+\tfrac16+\tfrac2{60}+\tfrac2{360}+\tfrac1{10800} =\tfrac{18421}{10800}, and the two coefficients 22 carry the whole content of the regrouping on this box. Where the running LCMs are pairwise distinct the identity is a relabelling.

Multiplying block radices along a run of blocks gives the product of the prime multipliers at the jumps in that run: for instance b1b2=60b_1b_2=60 is the product of the four multipliers at 3,4,5,83,4,5,8. Block 44 is the only one among the first six containing an internal power of each odd prime, whereas block 55 contains neither, so its radix falls back to the terminal factor alone.

The product-growth law gives a necessary lower bound on a possible length of such a segment, not a distribution law for residues or first successful lengths. No generic-residue model is used as evidence for the residue inequality at arbitrarily late starts.

Source inventory

The table gives declaration locations at their recorded revisions. Section 12.5 explains the assumptions attached to each kind of association. Before using the table, two conventions require attention: integer division at the initial index and removal of the first block. The Lean version of the normalising factor hah_a is a natural number computed by integer division: its value at 00 is 00, whereas h0=1/2h_0=1/2. It agrees with hah_a for a≥1a\ge1, as the identity for half the running LCM assumes. The Lean version of the tail XaX_a divides after casting to ℝ\mathbb R, so agrees with Xa=haTaX_a=h_aT_a at every index.

The denominator-clearing lemmas and the lemmas on division of an integer recurrence assume T1T_1 rational. The first block consists of 11 alone, so T1=S−1T_1=S-1; thus S=N/DS=N/D supplies T1=N−DD,gcd⁡(N−D,D)=gcd⁡(N,D).T_1=\frac{N-D}{D},\qquad \gcd(N-D,D)=\gcd(N,D). Lean proves this translation, which preserves the denominator, its smooth factor and the clearing onset.

Dependencies and remaining questions

The table separates the established special cases from the ordinary generalisations awaiting formalisation and the unresolved repeated-sum condition. Exact kernel rank concerns separation of a function; the residue criterion concerns a scalar sum and still needs arithmetic existence for its segments.

Result Dependency and limit
Running LCMs and intervals of constancy Prime-power divisibility and unique factorisation. Their geometry alone gives no irrationality statement.
Two-prime values Earlier factorisation plus the cited external Hecke–Mahler value theorem. The reduction to that theorem is checked in Lean; the theorem itself is a cited input (Section 14).
Distinct values, every PP Integrality of the scaled tails, rearranged chains at a return of the logarithmic flow, Kronecker’s theorem and an Euler characteristic count on a two-dimensional subtorus. Ordinary proof checked by a second agent; no Lean proof. It stops for the repeated sums because their scaled tails are unbounded.
Prime-power subseries The same two-tail comparison with the integer fpf_p and a chain chosen near the origin of the torus; no two-wall lemma. Ordinary proof checked by a second agent; no Lean proof. Says nothing about the whole repeated sum.
Distinct values, blocks Dyadic blocks, finitely many affine maps with disjoint images, integrality of the scaled tails and the irrationality of log⁡p/log⁡q\log p/\log q. The theorem for {2,3,5}\{2,3,5\} is checked in Lean; the general criterion has an ordinary proof, and Remark 5.8 adds exact finite computations. No statement about the repeated sums.
Arbitrary-order rank Diagonal rescaling, separate one-dimensional densities and a staircase determinant; checked in Lean.
Tail recurrence Counting the original multiplicities, normalising by half the boundary running LCM, and convergence; an abstract recurrence would not identify the sum.
Denominator reduction A finite prefix with cleared denominators and an upper bound for positive integer tails. The first valid index is determined exactly (Proposition 9.4); checked in Lean.
Residue criterion The actual recurrence, a dominating bound and segment products comparable to 8h8^h; the inequality at arbitrarily late starts remains unproved.
Weighted differences Exact reindexing and the contributions of the new boundary strips; integer enumeration checks the displayed counterexample to third-difference cancellation.
Finite computations Direct checks settle only their individual segments. The two large exclusions have published witnesses and exact checkers, and the larger scan a published saved run; none is a theorem input.

None of these results proves irrationality of the repeated sum ℛP\mathcal R_P for three or more primes.

The formal two-prime reduction

The source note in Section 12.5 distinguishes ordinary proofs from individual formal associations. For Theorem 1.2, the Lean development verifies the reduction of that theorem to the transcendence of the Hecke–Mahler boundary sum at an irrational θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and nonzero algebraic β,α\beta,\alpha with |β|<1|\beta|<1 and |β||α|θ<1|\beta||\alpha|^\theta<1, which is Theorem 1.1 of Bugeaud and Laurent [15] in the case ρ=0\rho=0, due to Loxton and van der Poorten [16]. Lean does not prove that input; the Lean theorem assumes it. The formal development checks the following parts of the reduction: the running least-common-multiple identity, the selection of the single power of qq between consecutive powers of pp, the factorisation of the repeated sum, the identification of the distinct running values, the telescoping identity, the boundary identity [long269:eq:hecke-mahler-boundary] expressing AA through the Hecke–Mahler sum, the irrationality of log⁡p/log⁡q\log p/\log q, and each side condition verified before the value theorem is applied. The two identities expressing 𝒟{p,q}\mathcal D_{\{p,q\}} and ℛ{p,q}\mathcal R_{\{p,q\}} as polynomials in AA are unconditional and carry no additional input.

A theorem whose own statement is conditional is formalised exactly as stated. Theorem 1.2 is asserted unconditionally in this record, and its Lean counterpart carries the additional named input described here.
